subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Neptune: The Windiest World
description: A quick win: understand Neptune: The Windiest World.

hook.text: Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system—over 2,000 km/h. No one expected that so far out.

buildup.text: It orbits 4.5 billion km from the Sun. One trip around takes 165 years to complete.

discovery.text: Neptune was found by math, not telescopes. Astronomers predicted its position from wobbles in Uranus's orbit.

twist.text: Its moon Triton orbits backward—the only large moon to do so. It was likely captured from the Kuiper Belt.

climax.text: Neptune emits 2.6 times more heat than it gets from the Sun. Its internal engine drives those winds.

punchline.text: Found by math, powered from within. The distant mystery.

quiz.question: How was Neptune discovered?
options: Mathematicians predicted its location from wobbles in Uranus's orbit
A powerful telescope spotted it by accident in 1846
Voyager 2 found it while passing through the outer solar system

details.summary: Neptune, the most distant planet, has the solar system's fastest winds — exceeding 2,100 km/h. Despite receiving minimal solar energy 4.5 billion kilometers from the Sun, Neptune is intensely dynamic with storms, dark spots, and internal heat exceeding what it receives from the Sun.
details.whyItMatters: Neptune's extreme winds and active weather powered by internal heat, despite minimal solar input, challenge our understanding of atmospheric dynamics.
takeaways: Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system at 2,100+ km/h
It radiates more internal heat than it receives from the Sun
Its large moon Triton may be a captured Kuiper Belt object

faq.question: How can Neptune have such fast winds with so little solar energy?
faq.answer: Neptune generates 2.6 times more heat than it receives from the Sun, possibly from slow gravitational contraction or chemical processes. This internal energy drives atmospheric circulation.

faq.question: Why is Triton special?
faq.answer: Triton orbits Neptune backward (retrograde), suggesting it was captured from the Kuiper Belt. It has nitrogen geysers erupting 8 km high, a thin atmosphere, and may hide a subsurface ocean. It's geologically active despite being -235°C. NASA has proposed a Triton flyby mission called Trident.
